title: Building DocuClear AI: Autonomous Enterprise Contract Risk Auditor & Real-time Redline Engine
author: bonthupraveen1
summary: Building DocuClear AI: Autonomous Enterprise Contract Risk Auditor & Real-time Redline Engine Enterprise procurement and legal teams spend an average of 4.5 hours manually reviewing single Master Services Agreements (MSAs). Over 68% of small-to-midsize businesses end up signing agreements containing uncapped indemnities, one-sided liability waivers, or severe IP transfer clauses—leading to average dispute losses exceeding $120,000. To solve this, I architected and built DocuClear AI : an autonomous contract risk auditor that ingests enterprise legal documents, maps clause topology, computes a deterministic risk telemetry score, and outputs legally protective counter-clauses in seconds. Recently, DocuClear AI was shortlisted in the Top 350 out of 50,000+ applicants nationwide at Hack With Hyderabad 3.0 (hosted by Devnovate at the Microsoft Hyderabad Campus). Here is a breakdown of the architecture, engineering design choices, and technical challenges solved. 🏗️ System Architecture Overview The application is structured into a decoupled client-server architecture designed for high-throughput document processing and zero hallucination: Frontend / Telemetry UI: Built with React and Next.js , utilizing high-contrast visual cues to surface critical clauses via a dynamic Red-Flag Heatmap . Backend API: Built on FastAPI (Python) , managing multipart PDF uploads, asynchronous extraction tasks, and deterministic AI parsing. AI & Extraction Engine: Integrated with Azure Document Intelligence for structural document layout analysis and Azure OpenAI (GPT-4o) for deterministic clause auditing. ⚙️ Core Technical Challenges & Solutions 1. Eliminating Hallucinations via Deterministic JSON Schemas Standard conversational LLMs tend to paraphrase or introduce synthetic legal obligations when asked to redline contracts. For enterprise legal workflows, nondeterministic behavior is a fatal flaw. To enforce strict determinism: The inference pipeline locks model temperature at 0.1 . Responses are forced into rigid Pydantic schemas enforcing explicit classification tiers: CRITICAL , WARNING , and SAFE . Instead of open-ended text generation, counter-clauses are extractive replacements generated strictly against predefined enterprise risk taxonomies (e.g., standard trailing 12-month liability caps and mutual indemnification). python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import List, Literal class RedlineAudit(BaseModel): clause_id: str section_name: str risk_level: Literal["CRITICAL", "WARNING", "SAFE"] original_clause: str flagged_issue: str balanced_counter_clause: str rationale: str class ContractAuditResponse(BaseModel): document_name: str aggregate_risk_score: int = Field(ge=0, le=100) audit_findings: List[RedlineAudit]

title: Our deploys sent SIGTERM. Our workers only ever got SIGKILL.
author: Pierre-Laurent Medori
summary: On October 20, right after a deploy, I ran our queue-count command. The registry of started jobs in our main queue listed 27 jobs. No worker was running any of them. Every one had been killed by a deploy. The next morning, a worker died while cleaning up after four jobs killed by that morning's deploy. It was idle, so no job was lost, and the pool started a new one. Following that crash led back to a line we thought we had fixed in May. Some context. I run engineering at GoodBarber , an app platform. Our AI app builder writes the code of an app section from a description, and each generation runs as a job on a pool of RQ workers: rq 2.12, started with django-rq's rqworker-pool , with the tasks declared through django-tasks. It all runs in Docker Compose on two hosts, and a deploy takes the containers down, then brings the new image up. This post is about what those deploys were doing to the workers and the four fixes we shipped on October 22. The same deploy changed what the jobs are made of: our queue stopped carrying pickle. PID 1 was bash Our worker containers run a short shell script. Until October 22, it ended like this: exec python manage.py rqworker-pool \ --job-class django_tasks_rq.Job \ --num-workers " ${ NUM_WORKERS } " \ ${ QUEUES } \ 2>&1 | tee -a " ${ LOGFILE } " The exec is there so that Python replaces the shell and receives the signals. In a pipeline, it can't. Bash runs each side of a pipe in a subshell, so the exec replaced a subshell, and the script's own bash stayed PID 1 of the container, waiting for both sides of the pipeline to finish. docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1. Our bash ignored it and passed nothing on, so nothing happened until the 15 seconds of stop_grace_period ran out. Then Docker sent SIGKILL, and every process in the container died with it. Every stop ended that way, and so did every deploy. The fix gives the log a tee of its own and lets Python take the script's place: exec > >( tee -a " ${ LOGFILE } " ) 2>&1 exec python manage.py rqworker-pool \ --job-class django_tasks_rq.Job \ --num-workers " ${ NUM_WORKERS } " \ ${ QUEUES } Each worker service in the compose file also got init: true : command : ./deploy/common/rqworker.sh init : true stop_grace_period : 15s With it, Docker's small init process (tini) is PID 1. It hands SIGTERM to its child, now the Python process, and it reaps orphans. Python as PID 1 wouldn't, and a pool does leave orphans: when a worker is killed, the work horse it forked for a job is handed to PID 1. The history is the uncomfortable part. On May 28, we pushed two commits eleven minutes apart. The first cut the workers' grace period from 60 seconds to 15. Its message said deploys sat about 60 seconds in "Stopping" because the pool "stays blocked in Redis BLPOP until the grace expires, even when no jobs are in flight". The second removed a bash -c wrapper from the compose commands, with the right diagnosis: bash in PID 1 doesn't forward SIGTERM. It counted on each script's own exec to make the real process PID 1. The worker's exec sat in a pipeline, and as you'll see below, the web script had none. Bash moved from the wrapper to the shebang and stayed PID 1. The BLPOP explanation stayed in a comment above stop_grace_period for almost five months. We never checked what PID 1 was after the change. It takes one command: docker exec <container> cat /proc/1/comm Before the fix, the answer on our workers was bash . The new test doesn't take the script's word for it either. It runs the real script with a fake python and sends SIGTERM to the script. It passes only if the fake python has become the script's own process and exits on the signal with its own exit code. All three of its cases fail on the old script. Now that SIGTERM arrives, the pool stops its workers: an idle worker exits at once, and its scheduler gives back its lock. A job still running when the 15 seconds end still dies in the SIGKILL, and our generations take between 85 and 500 seconds, so a deploy still kills every generation in flight. The web container had the same bug, and uWSGI has its own idea of SIGTERM The script of our web container started uWSGI without exec . Bash stayed PID 1 and ignored SIGTERM, so uWSGI was killed at the end of Compose's default 10-second stop timeout. The comment above it in the compose file described an exec the script didn't have. Adding exec wasn't enough. We measured each variant in our image, with two 5-second requests in flight when docker stop arrived: Script What docker stop got no exec (before) 10.3 s, exit code 137: SIGKILL exec uwsgi uWSGI 2.0 treats SIGTERM as a "brutal reload": it reloaded its workers, cut both requests, and the stop still ended in SIGKILL exec and --die-on-term 2.4 s, exit code 0, both requests cut exec and --hook-master-start "unix_signal:15 gracefully_kill_them_all" 4.7 s, exit code 0, both requests got their 200 We kept the last line. A request that fits in the stop timeout is now served to the end, and a longer one still dies in the SIGKILL. Its test had a trap of its own. The first version sent SIGTERM half a second after starting a 2-second request. Under load, the signal could land before the request had entered the application, and the test failed for nothing, or after the request had ended, and the test passed without ever stopping uWSGI mid-request. The test application now writes a file as soon as a request enters it, and the test waits for that file before it sends the signal. The job nobody was running A SIGKILL leaves traces in Redis. RQ keeps a registry of started jobs for each queue, stored under rq:wip:<queue> . When a worker dies in the middle of a job, the job's entry stays there with nothing behind it, and once the entry expires, a maintenance pass is supposed to mark the job as failed and run its failure callback. That maintenance pass was what crashed. django-rq's rqworker-pool builds its queues with our job class, but RQ's WorkerPool , which it starts, passes each child only the queue names, and the child rebuilds the queues with RQ's base Job class, whatever --job-class says. The cleanup reads abandoned jobs with the queue's job class. Our jobs come from django-tasks, whose RQ backend registers a failure callback that reads job.task_result , an attribute only its own Job subclass has. Read as a base Job , every abandoned job made the callback raise: AttributeError: 'Job' object has no attribute 'task_result' The error escaped the worker's loop. The child died with the job still marked "started", and the queue's maintenance lock stayed taken for 15 minutes, until the next child ran the same cleanup and died on the same job. As long as those entries were there, we lost a worker about every quarter of an hour. The workers were idle each time, so no job was lost, and the pool replaced them. Our workaround was to delete the entries by hand after each deploy, with a ZREMRANGEBYSCORE on rq:wip:default . The fix is a few lines in a mixin on our worker class. It gives the child's queues the worker's job class, as RQ does when a worker is handed queue names: class PoolWorkerMixin : def __init__ ( self , queues , * args , ** kwargs ): super (). __init__ ( queues , * args , ** kwargs ) for queue in self . queues : queue . job_class = self . job_class An abandoned job is now failed the way RQ intends: its callback runs, and the job moves from the started registry to the failed one. The manual cleanup isn't needed anymore. The scheduler that took almost 14 minutes to come back The SIGKILL left one more thing behind. Every child of the pool starts RQ's scheduler, but only the one holding the queue's scheduler lock actually runs it. The lock is a Redis key, rq:scheduler-lock:<queue> , that lives 61 seconds and is refreshed every second. A scheduler killed along with its worker leaves the key to expire on its own. RQ 2.12 tries the lock again when a worker starts, which right after a restart is too early since the dead lock is still there, and after that only during maintenance: every 10 minutes, which an idle worker checks between two waits of 405 seconds. We measured it in our image. After a docker kill and a restart, a job due a few seconds later left the scheduled registry 815 seconds after the kill. Retries and the jobs we chain on a timer all waited that long after any deploy that ended in SIGKILL, which until then meant every deploy. The same mixin now tries the lock every 10 seconds while its worker has no scheduler running: between short waits when the worker is idle, and at the 30-second heartbeat of the job it watches when it's busy. It never takes a lock that a live scheduler holds, and it stops trying once the worker has been asked to stop, otherwise a busy worker could grab the lock during the grace period and leave it to the SIGKILL. With the patch, the same job left 64 seconds after the kill, 3 seconds after the dead lock expired. With the pool's only slot busy, it left after 67 seconds. Then we changed what the jobs are made of The four fixes went out on the morning of October 22. The same deploy turned on a change we had prepared a few days earlier: the queue stopped carrying pickle. RQ serializes jobs with pickle by default, and unpickles a job before anything checks what it is. With pickle, anything that can write to the Redis a worker reads from can make that worker run code. JSON closes that. It can't be rolled out gradually, though: a job can only be read in the format it was written in, and a worker reads every job in its queues with a single serializer. A few choices shaped the switch. No fallback reader. Trying JSON first and pickle when it fails would have kept pickle.loads on whatever Redis holds, which is exactly what we were removing. So the switch happens with the queues drained, and a job left in pickle fails without being read. The worker takes its serializer from the queue. rqworker and rqworker-pool have a --serializer option that defaults to pickle. With two settings that have to agree, every job fails the first time they don't, so our worker class reads the serializer from the queue's configuration and ignores the flag. The queues the pool rebuilds also come with RQ's default serializer, pickle, so the same class sets the configured one on each of them, as the mixin above does for the job class. A test builds a pool child exactly the way RQ does and checks both. A strict serializer instead of RQ's JSON one. RQ's JSON serializer silently turns integer keys into strings, because that's what json.dumps does. Ours refuses what JSON would change or can't carry: non-string keys, bytes, NaN, infinities, UUIDs, datetimes. Tuples are the one exception it lets through, as lists, since django-tasks already normalizes arguments that way. Its error names where the value is and its type, never the value itself. A test that reads every enqueue site. It parses our code to find the 22 places in 15 files that enqueue a task, then round-trips each argument through JSON. A new task or a new call site fails the test until someone adds it. Review caught the trap we had missed. When a scheduled job comes due, RQ writes it back, metadata included, as it moves it to the queue. A job scheduled in pickle before the switch has metadata that JSON can't read, which RQ keeps as raw bytes, and writing that back raises. The whole batch of due jobs is then never written, and the scheduler process dies, again at every restart. One leftover job would have held back every job due with it. Our scheduler now moves such jobs to the failed registry first, without reading them, before RQ queues the rest. The stats command had a trap too. In RQ, counting a registry runs its cleanup first, and django-rq's rqstats builds its registries without the queue's serializer, so running it could unpickle whatever an expired entry holds. We count our queues with a small management command of our own that never reads a job. The switch itself took a short checklist. Clear the abandoned entries, then wait until the count command reports every queue drained, with nothing queued, started, deferred or scheduled. Turn the setting on and build once. Deploy both hosts back to back, because between the two deploys, a job written in one format and read by a worker of the other fails without running. After the deploy, the queues reported the JSON serializer, and the first check of the logs found no DeserializationError and no traceback. Both hosts showed zero abandoned started jobs and zero overdue scheduled jobs. A race in the deploy script The deploy script had a race of its own. It runs docker compose down -v , which removes the volumes our two web containers share, and the next up -d recreates them empty. Docker copies the image's files into an empty named volume when a container that mounts it starts, and both containers started at the same moment. We first saw the failure on October 12 and wrote it down as unrelated to the code. At 15:19 on October 22, one of the two containers hit failed to mkdir …/_data/admin: file exists and up -d stopped there. The host ran without a single container for three minutes, until the deploy was launched again. Replayed locally with the old script, the race broke 2 deploys out of 20. The fix starts one web container alone right after down -v , then the rest. Docker only copies into an empty volume, so the second container finds the files already there, and 60 local deploys out of 60 went through. It reached production on the morning of October 26. The deploy script runs git pull on its own repository, and bash keeps executing the copy of the script it opened before the pull. On the second host, that old copy hit the race one last time, and the run after it, on the new script, started all six containers. What a deploy still breaks A generation running during a deploy still dies. The pool now gets SIGTERM and waits for the job, but a generation needs minutes and the grace period is 15 seconds. A grace period longer than our slowest generation, around 500 seconds, would save it, and every docker stop could then take more than eight minutes. What I'd check in your own setup Run docker exec <container> cat /proc/1/comm on every container that runs jobs or serves requests. If it prints bash or sh , docker stop most likely ends in SIGKILL there. A trap in the script won't save it: bash runs a trap only after the foreground command returns, so the process would have to run in the background behind a wait . exec is simpler. Look for exec inside a pipeline. exec cmd | tee log doesn't replace the shell. After a deploy, count the entries in your started-job registries that no live worker is running. Each one is a job the deploy killed. If you run uWSGI 2.0, check what it does with SIGTERM before you rely on it to stop. If your deploy script updates itself with git pull , its first run after a change is still the old script. If your jobs run for minutes, what happens to them when you deploy: do you drain the queue first, or let them die and retry?

title: I read ~150 public Razorpay webhook handlers. At least 9 would process the same payment twice.
author: Pritom Mazumdar
summary: Razorpay delivers webhooks "at least once". Its own docs say the same event can arrive more than once and tell you to dedupe on x-razorpay-event-id . I wanted to see how often real code actually does that. Method. I pulled 247 public Python / JS / TS files on GitHub that reference Razorpay webhook events. A keyword scan flagged 48 candidates, and each one was then reviewed line by line. About 148 files contain a real webhook handler; the rest are helpers, schemas or client-side "verify payment" endpoints. I only counted a handler if delivering the same event twice would demonstrably run a non-idempotent side effect twice. Where idempotency could come from a database constraint I couldn't see, I marked it unclear rather than broken. (I'm being strict here because my first keyword-only pass said "1 in 5". When I read the code, most of those were false alarms, e.g. a wallet field that just stores the payment method.) What I found At least 9 of ~148 handlers (6%) run a side effect again when the same webhook is redelivered. Another 7 are unclear. (Only the 48 flagged files were checked for this, so the real number can only be higher.) 5 of those 9 change money-like values: user.wallet = (user.wallet || 0) + 100 on every payment.captured . Razorpay retries, and the user gets 200 coins. invoice.amount_paid_paise += amount and a customer "total recovered" counter, both incremented on every delivery. A WorkerPayout row created on every payment.captured . That's a duplicate payout record, and this handler doesn't verify signatures either. 9 handlers (6%) never verify the webhook signature at all. Anyone who finds the URL can POST a fake payment.captured . Several more verify only when the header or secret is present, so leaving the secret unset silently disables the check. A common, subtler pattern: computing the HMAC over JSON.stringify(req.body) instead of the raw request body. It works until something re-serializes the JSON differently, and then valid webhooks start failing. 6% doesn't sound like much until you remember these are the people who publish their payment code. And it only takes one retry storm to double-pay every affected user. Why tests don't catch it. Everyone tests the happy path once in Razorpay test mode. Nobody fires the same event three times, or sends events out of order. What I built. carbon-layer is an open-source CLI that fires realistic, correctly signed Razorpay, Stripe, Cashfree, Juspay and Hyperswitch webhooks at your local endpoint, including retries with the same X-Razorpay-Event-Id , out-of-order delivery, and bad signatures. A non-idempotent handler still answers 200, so it also checks the side effect itself: give it any command that counts what your handler does, and it compares before and after. pip install -U carbon-layer carbon run dispute-spike --provider razorpay \ --webhook-url http://localhost:8000/webhooks --webhook-secret $SECRET \ --webhook-repeat 3 --webhook-order random \ --verify-cmd "psql -tAc 'select count(*) from wallet_credits'" Against a handler written like the wallet one above: FAIL: duplicate processing: payment.captured: 200 unique events caused 600 side effects; handler is not idempotent The same handler with an event-id check gives PASS: each event processed exactly once . No gateway account needed. Repo: github.com/Pritom14/carbon-layer The fix most of these handlers need: record x-razorpay-event-id in a table with a UNIQUE constraint, in the same transaction as the side effect. If the event is already there, return 200 and do nothing: create table processed_webhooks ( event_id text primary key , received_at timestamptz default now ()); app . post ( ' /webhooks/razorpay ' , express . raw ({ type : ' application/json ' }), async ( req , res ) => { if ( ! Razorpay . validateWebhookSignature ( req . body . toString (), req . get ( ' x-razorpay-signature ' ), SECRET )) return res . sendStatus ( 400 ); // verify the RAW body, not JSON.stringify(req.body) const eventId = req . get ( ' x-razorpay-event-id ' ); const event = JSON . parse ( req . body ); await db . tx ( async ( t ) => { const { rowCount } = await t . query ( ' insert into processed_webhooks (event_id) values ($1) on conflict do nothing ' , [ eventId ]); if ( rowCount === 0 ) return ; // duplicate delivery: already handled if ( event . event === ' payment.captured ' ) await creditWallet ( t , event . payload . payment . entity ); }); res . sendStatus ( 200 ); }); Doing the insert and the side effect in one transaction matters: if the credit fails, the event id rolls back too, and Razorpay's retry gets processed properly. (Repo names are deliberately left out. If you want to know whether yours was in the scan, DM me and I'll send you the specific finding privately.)

title: I built a free mafia browser game with Next.js, and I'm looking for testers
author: Movetio
summary: Hi dev.to, I'm a solo developer, and this is my first game. It's called Movetio : a free, text-based mafia game that runs in your browser. It's now in an open test until 14 November 2026 , and I'd really appreciate a few more people trying it and telling me honestly what works and what doesn't. This isn't a launch post. The game is unfinished, and that's the point of the test. What the game is Movetio is a classic text-based game. You pick actions, watch your numbers change, and slowly build up your position in the city. Right now you can: Do crimes. Crimes cost energy. You use it to earn cash and climb the ranks, and when it runs out you have to choose what to do next. Run smuggling routes. You move goods between Rotterdam, Amsterdam and The Hague . Your cargo space is limited, so you have to choose which loads are worth carrying. Join a family. Players team up in families that share a bank, compete on a leaderboard and have their own public page. Plan heists. Family members plan a heist together, and each person picks a role: Muscle, Driver, Lookout or Fixer . Visit the casino. There's blackjack and roulette. You can own a table yourself or try to bankrupt the bank. It uses in-game money only. There's no real-money gambling. Watch out for PvP. Other players are your rivals, so keep your money safe. You can play in English, Dutch, Brazilian Portuguese, Polish and Spanish , in the browser on your phone or desktop. Why Next.js and the browser I wanted the game to be as easy as possible to try. With a browser game there's nothing to download or install and no store to go through. You open a link, and it works on both your phone and your laptop. A text-based game also fits the web well. Most of it is pages, forms, lists and numbers, which is what the web has always done well. Next.js let me keep the pages and the game logic in one project, and as a solo developer that matters a lot. I can make a change, test it on my phone and on desktop, and ship it without juggling separate apps. I'm still learning a lot along the way. Not every decision I made early on was the right one, and the open test is partly about finding out where that shows. What I'd love feedback on This is where I could really use your help. You don't need to play for hours. Even a short session gives me useful information. The first few minutes. Is it clear what to do when you start? Where did you get stuck or feel lost? Pacing and balance. Do crimes and energy feel rewarding, or grindy? Do the smuggling routes and cargo choices feel meaningful? Families and heists. If you play with a friend or two, does planning a heist with roles make sense? Is the shared bank clear? Mobile. Does everything fit on your screen? Are buttons easy to tap? Is anything slow or broken? Language. If you play in a language other than English, does the text read naturally? Typos and odd phrasing are very welcome reports. Bugs. Anything that breaks, looks wrong or behaves strangely. You can report things with the bug report option in the game, or just leave a comment below. Honest or even harsh feedback is more useful to me than polite silence. How to join Play in your browser: https://movetio.com Sign-up is free and needs an email account . The game is 18+ , with one account per person. The open test runs until 14 November 2026 . Balance, pacing and clarity are all still being tuned, so what testers say during these weeks directly decides what I work on next. Thanks Building a game alone is exciting, but it's easy to lose perspective when you're the only one who has ever played it. If you have a few minutes, I'd be very grateful if you tried it and told me what you think. I'll read and answer every comment. Thanks for reading, and maybe see you in the city.

title: How do AI agents pay for an API?
author: ScriptMasterLabs
summary: How do AI agents pay for an API? An AI agent pays when a server sends a 402 challenge. It signs the exact request, retries, and the PAYMENT-RESPONSE header is its receipt. The steps, in order The agent asks for a page or a data call. The server replies with HTTP 402 instead of data. The 402 header lists price, currency, and network. Here the price is 0.001 USDC per accepted read. The network is Base, chain eip155:8453. The protocol is x402 version 2. The agent signs a payment for that exact amount. It sends the same request again with proof attached. A facilitator checks the payment and settles it on Base. The server then returns the data it promised. The reply carries a PAYMENT-RESPONSE header as the receipt. One real job, with real numbers ScriptMasterLabs has published settlement observations since September 2, 2026. Those records counted 96 settlements on Base through October 6, 2026. Most early settlements were owner self-tests, not customer sales. A live probe found a 402 reply in 0.67 seconds. That reply quoted 0.001 USDC for one read. Failed reads cost nothing under those terms. What the 402 is not The 402 is the price tag, not the receipt. No money has moved when 402 first appears. Money moves only after signing and settlement succeed. The PAYMENT-RESPONSE header is the receipt after settlement. What an agent needs first An agent needs a wallet with USDC on Base. It needs code that reads x402 v2 challenges. It needs a spending cap set before work starts. No account or API key is needed here. No human checkout step sits in the loop. title: DeepTutor: A Chinese Translation of the HKUDS Tutoring Agent, and What It Actually Saves You
author: sun young
summary: The original README for HKUDS/DeepTutor is long. Long enough that a reader whose English is serviceable but not fast will bounce off it before reaching the install steps. That is the problem the Chinese translation at yangshun2005/DeepTutor-cn tries to solve, and it is a narrower problem than "make the project accessible" — worth being precise about. The original project: 48925 stars, written in Python, Apache-2.0 licensed. Topics listed are ai-agents, ai-tutor, clawbot, cli-tool, deepresearch. Its own one-line description is "Lifelong Personalized Tutoring." The Chinese version was published today and has zero stars. Nothing in this article should be read as a claim that the translation has traction; it doesn't yet. What the translation actually contains The repository is structured around two distinct pieces of text, and the distinction matters: A translated version of the original README ( README_en.md holds the English original). The stated intent is fidelity to the source — "力求忠于原文." A supplementary Chinese quick-start guide at the top of the page, explicitly marked as not part of the original document ("非原文内容"). Its purpose is to get you from zero to a running instance without reading the full README. That second part is the interesting one. A pure translation of a 3000-line README still leaves you reading 3000 lines. The quick-start is a different artifact: a curated path through the project for someone who wants to evaluate it in fifteen minutes. The translation is dated 2026-10-29. The README invites issues and PRs for inaccuracies, which is the right posture — translations of fast-moving projects rot quickly, and this one will too. Why a Chinese README is worth more than it sounds For a project like this, the documentation is not a wrapper around the code. It is where most of the design decisions live. Look at the release history in the README. Between v1.6.3 and v1.7.0 the project shipped, among other things: a breaking frontend/backend refactor, learner and guardian accounts, bounded tutoring memory, resumable embedding checkpoints, a Mastery Path mode with gated tools, LightRAG character models, Kiwix archives, per-model API capability declarations, and a single exec tool unified across languages. Each of those is a paragraph or two in the changelog. Reading them in a second language, at speed, while also trying to understand the architecture, is where comprehension quietly fails. The failure mode isn't total. You get the gist. But you miss the qualifiers — the "bounded" in bounded memory, the "gated" in gated tools, the "explicit" in explicit per-model capabilities. Those words carry the actual engineering constraints. A reader working in a second language tends to skim past them and then wonder why the system behaves unexpectedly. The Chinese version's value is concentrated here: it lets a Chinese-speaking developer read the constraints at full resolution instead of at 70%. The quick-start path The supplementary guide states the Python requirement plainly: 3.11 or above, per pyproject.toml ( >=3.11 ). That is the first thing to check, and it is the kind of detail that gets buried in an English README's prerequisites section. The original README's own navigation reflects the project's shape: 功能特性 · 快速开始 · 探索 DeepTutor · CLI · 生态 · 社区 In English: features, quick start, exploring DeepTutor, CLI, ecosystem (EduHub and a skills community), community. That ordering is informative. The CLI section gets its own top-level slot — the README labels it "agent 原生接口," agent-native interface. If you are coming from a web-app mental model, that is the part to read first, because it tells you what the system considers its primary surface. What the project is, structurally From the README and the pyproject.toml description, DeepTutor describes itself as an agent-native personalized learning companion with multi-agent collaboration and RAG. The pieces it integrates into a single learning workspace: Document parsing Knowledge base retrieval Practice and assessment Voice and video reading That is a wide surface. The changelog confirms the width — releases mention exercise generation from original sources, question banks, reading folders with in-chat selection actions, paginated Office previews, chart images sent to vision models, native Gemini voice, Polish/German/French/Ukrainian interfaces, and a research toolset. A project this broad has a real onboarding cost, and documentation is the main lever on that cost. This is the argument for the translation, and it is a modest argument, not a dramatic one. It removes a language tax. It does not remove the complexity. Reading the changelog as a design document One practical suggestion for anyone evaluating DeepTutor through the Chinese version: read the release notes before the feature list. The v1.6.7 entry is a list of fixes — whole books collapsing into empty chapters, quizzes producing no output, model drafts leaking into body text, formulas printing as raw source, unsubmittable cards. v1.6.6 mentions unsubmittable answers, a copy button that lied, Docker-internal Codex login, and a 100 KB reduction on the homepage route. These are not marketing entries. They tell you what breaks under load and what the maintainers prioritize. A translated changelog is arguably more useful than a translated feature list, because feature lists translate cleanly (the nouns survive) while bug descriptions carry the specific texture of what went wrong. Caveats The translation is one day old. Expect drift: the original ships releases at a pace of roughly one every few days based on the dates in the README (v1.6.3 through v1.7.0 span September 2 to October 28). The Chinese README will lag. The quick-start is a supplement, not a substitute. If you hit something the guide doesn't cover, the English original is authoritative, and README_en.md is right there in the same repository. And a translation is only as good as its review. The repository says as much. If you find a term rendered badly — "有界辅导记忆" for bounded tutoring memory is a reasonable choice, but reasonable choices are still choices — file an issue. Where to look Chinese version: https://github.com/yangshun2005/DeepTutor-cn Original: https://github.com/HKUDS/DeepTutor Project site: https://deeptutor.info/ If you are a Chinese-speaking developer who has been putting off trying DeepTutor because the README is a wall of English, the translation removes that specific excuse. The rest of the work — Python 3.11, the CLI, the knowledge base setup — is unchanged, and no translation makes it smaller. Chinese documentation: https://github.com/yangshun2005/DeepTutor-cn I'm an independent enterprise AI delivery consultant — private LLM deployment, RAG, agent workflows, AIOps. title: Flaky Tests Are Slowing Down Every Release: Here's How to Fix Them
author: vivek
summary: The build fails. You re-run it. It passes. Nobody investigates, and the team moves on. That small ritual is how flaky tests quietly drain a team. A flaky test passes and fails on the same code, so every failure becomes a question: is this a real bug, or just noise? Once engineers stop trusting the answer, the whole test suite loses its value. Why tests turn flaky Brittle selectors: A renamed button or a restructured page breaks tests that were never really wrong. Timing issues: Hard-coded waits and race conditions between the UI and the backend. Shared or unstable test data: Tests that depend on state left behind by other tests. Environment drift: Differences between local machines, CI runners, and staging. Third-party dependencies: External APIs and services that respond slowly or inconsistently. The real cost Flaky tests are not just annoying. Every re-run slows the pipeline, every false alarm pulls an engineer away from real work, and every ignored failure raises the odds that a genuine bug reaches production. Over time, teams either spend their sprints maintaining scripts or stop relying on automation altogether. How to fix it Quarantine and track. Isolate known flaky tests so they stop blocking releases, and measure how often each one fails. Fix the root cause. Replace fixed waits with condition-based waits, and give every test its own clean data. Stabilize the environment. Keep CI and staging consistent and mock unreliable third-party calls. Reduce maintenance at the source. Most flakiness comes from scripts that break when the product changes. This is where an [AI-powered test automation platform] helps: [self-healing tests] adapt when the interface changes instead of failing on every UI tweak. Write tests in plain language. With BotGauge , teams can describe scenarios in plain English and let AI handle test generation and execution, so coverage grows without a pile of fragile scripts to maintain. Run it on every change. Plug your suite into your pipeline with [automated regression testing] so problems surface while the change is still fresh. Takeaway A test suite is only useful if you trust it. Cut the noise, and a failing test becomes a signal worth acting on.

Calling it https://api.callirra.com , bearer key, two calls: create, then poll. const headers = { authorization : `Bearer ${ process . env . CALLIRRA_API_KEY } ` , ' content-type ' : ' application/json ' , }; const created = await fetch ( ' https://api.callirra.com/v1/videos ' , { method : ' POST ' , headers , body : JSON . stringify ({ model : ' minimax-h3 ' , mode : ' image_to_video ' , prompt : ' Slow push in as the wind lifts the scarf; the camera settles on the eyes. ' , resolution : ' 768p ' , duration_seconds : 5 , aspect_ratio : ' 16:9 ' , frame_images : [ ' https://example.com/ref-01.jpg ' ], }), }); const { job } = await created . json (); // { id, status, credits_reserved } let state ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < 120 ; i += 1 ) { const r = await fetch ( `https://api.callirra.com/v1/videos/ ${ job . id } ` , { headers }); state = ( await r . json ()). job ; if ([ ' completed ' , ' failed ' , ' cancelled ' , ' expired ' ]. includes ( state . status )) break ; await new Promise (( done ) => setTimeout ( done , 5000 )); } console . log ( state . status , state . content_url ); // signed URL, short lived credits_reserved comes back as a string of internal units; divide by 100 for public credits if you are building a cost display. Failure modes that cost me an afternoon content_policy is a real error code , and it refunds. H3 runs a provider-side safety check on the output; a rejected render bills nothing but does end the job. Aspect ratios are validated per scene, not per model. 1:1 at 1080P needs a reference image; 21:9 only exists at 2K. Duration is integer seconds. Fractional durations are rounded, which silently changes the price you quoted a user. Free-tier output is watermarked; paid output is not. If you build a demo on a free account, the watermark is a product decision, not a bug. What I would build with it Nine reference images plus three audio clips is enough to hold a character, a location, a wardrobe and a voice across a series of shots, which is the actual bottleneck in short-form production. The 480P tier at a cent a second is cheap enough to storyboard at volume, and 1080P at three cents is where you render the takes you keep. The full tier table and per-model quotes are at callirra.com/minimax-h3 , and the API contract at callirra.com/api . If something here does not match what the API returns today, tell me; I would rather correct the post than leave a wrong table on the internet.

title: When a data pipeline fails, can an AI agent explain why?
author: Artem Golub
summary: A data pipeline fails. You open the logs, find the failed run, check the input file, and try to work out what happened. Did the source send bad data? Did processing fail? Is the evidence you need even available? That investigation is the part I'm exploring with Hermes Data Reliability : a small AWS lab that uses Hermes Agent, built by Nous Research , to investigate failed data loads and propose a next step. The goal is to give an engineer something useful to review: an explanation, the evidence behind it, and an honest account of what remains unclear. Start with one broken file The example pipeline is deliberately simple: Producer Lambda -> S3 input -> SQS -> Processor Lambda -> S3 output The producer creates a JSON file containing five records. The processor checks that each record has a numeric amount , doubles it, and writes the result back to S3. For the failure scenario, the producer puts this in the third record: { "record_id" : 3 , "amount" : "not-a-number" } The processor rejects it during validation. Now there's a concrete failure to investigate, with a known answer we can compare the agent's explanation against. This small example keeps the investigation easy to follow. We can inspect the input, the processing attempt, and the logs without needing to understand a whole company's data platform first. From a log message to an investigation The workflow has three main parts. First, collect the signal. A collector reads configured CloudWatch logs and applies matching rules defined in YAML. When a rule matches, it saves an incident in SQLite. Then, investigate. A separate worker picks up the incident and starts Hermes. The agent chooses which available evidence to inspect within the permissions and limits set for that investigation. For a lab run, that can include nearby logs, the input file, and saved processing-attempt details. Finally, write up the findings. The report includes the failed stage, an explanation, uncertainty, a proposed action, and references to the evidence used. For the malformed record, a useful explanation would look something like this: Validation failed because the third record contains a string in amount , where the processor requires a number. Correct that value at the source and review how to reprocess the affected file. The available evidence does not establish that a corrected run has succeeded. That's an illustrative summary, rather than output from a measured live run. An actual report also needs references to evidence returned during its investigation. Why keep collection separate from the agent? The collector continues working while Hermes is busy or unavailable. Incidents and collection progress are saved in the database, so a restart can resume from saved state. This also gives ordinary code a clear job: read the configured sources, apply the rules, and queue the matches. The agent handles the investigation after a match. There are limits on investigation time, tool calls, and attempts. Interrupted and failed attempts still count. A difficult incident shouldn't create an endless loop of model calls. Give the agent evidence and clear boundaries The current investigation tools provide read-only access. Engineers decide which changes to make. Access is enforced by code outside the model. Each tool request is checked against the approved resources, time window, and remaining budget. AWS credentials stay outside the model container. The host also records which evidence each tool call returned. Before an automatic finding is accepted, its citations are checked against those records. That check has a specific purpose: confirm that the cited evidence was actually returned during this investigation. It cannot prove that the agent interpreted the evidence correctly. Reviewing the explanation still matters. Logs and file contents are treated as untrusted input, too. Text inside a log does not get to grant permissions or tell the agent to change its task. “I couldn't verify that” is useful information An investigation can run into missing permissions, unavailable input, or incomplete results. Those limitations belong in the report. A failed read doesn't establish that a file is missing. A partial search doesn't establish that no relevant event happened. The project includes three evaluation scenarios: a malformed record, a log containing misleading instructions, and an unavailable input file. They let us examine both the diagnosis and how the agent handles evidence it should distrust or cannot inspect. These are a starting point for evaluation. Broader reliability needs more cases and measured results. Where the project stands Today, the lab focuses on explicit failures found through configured CloudWatch log matches. Detection of silent stoppages and overdue output, along with Snowflake integration, is still future work. I'm building this to make the investigation after a pipeline failure easier: follow the evidence, explain what happened, and suggest a next step an engineer can review. I'd love to shape it around the problems you actually run into. If you work with data pipelines, which recurring failure would you want an agent to investigate first? Maybe it's a file that arrives late, a schema change that breaks a load, or a job that reports success while some data never reaches its destination. I'm looking for real examples I can recreate in the lab and run the agent against. Leave a comment below or open a GitHub issue . A short description is enough to start: What does your pipeline look like, and which tools does it use? What goes wrong, and how do you notice? What logs or other clues do you have, and how do you usually find the cause? A simplified setup or an anonymized example is perfect. I'd like to turn these into reproducible scenarios and test what the agent can explain, where it gets stuck, and what evidence would help it do better. Your recurring headache could help shape the next lab example. If this is useful to you, give the project a star on GitHub . It helps others discover it, and I'd appreciate the support.

title: Laravel AI Failover Worked. My JSON Contract Didn’t.
author: Paul-S
summary: A Laravel AI failover can produce a surprisingly successful failure. 09:42:11 primary_provider 429 rate_limit 09:42:12 fallback_provider 200 success 09:42:12 application Missing key: recommended_action The primary provider was unavailable. Laravel moved the request to the backup provider, which returned a valid response. Infrastructure saw success. The application crashed. The Prompt Was Pretending to Be a Contract The agent had been instructed to return JSON: Return JSON using this structure: { "risk": "low|medium|high", "recommended_action": "approve|review|reject", "reason": "string" } The primary model usually followed that instruction. The fallback model returned this instead: { "risk_level" : "medium" , "action" : "manual_review" , "explanation" : "The account requires additional verification." } Nothing about that answer was nonsensical. A person could understand it immediately. PHP could not. The parser expected recommended_action . The fallback supplied action . Even its value changed from review to manual_review . Failover had restored availability without preserving substitutability. Provider Failover Is Not Contract Failover The Laravel AI SDK allows an ordered list of providers: use Laravel\Ai\Enums\Lab ; $response = ( new RefundDecision ) -> prompt ( 'Evaluate refund request RF-1084.' , provider : [ Lab :: OpenAI , Lab :: Anthropic , ], ); If the primary provider is rate-limited or unavailable, the SDK can move to the next one. That answers one question: Can another provider complete the request? It does not automatically answer another: Will every provider behave identically enough for my application? Providers differ in model behavior, supported tools, configuration options, and structured-output implementations. Laravel hides much of the transport complexity, but the application still owns its business contract. The Laravel AI SDK’s recent changelog includes provider-specific structured-output fixes. That is a useful reminder that multi-provider compatibility must be tested, not assumed. Replace JSON Instructions With a Schema Laravel agents can implement HasStructuredOutput instead of asking for JSON in natural-language instructions. <?php namespace App\Ai\Agents ; use Illuminate\Contracts\JsonSchema\JsonSchema ; use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\Agent ; use Laravel\Ai\Contracts\HasStructuredOutput ; use Laravel\Ai\Promptable ; class RefundDecision implements Agent , HasStructuredOutput { use Promptable ; public function instructions (): string { return <<<'PROMPT' Evaluate the refund request. Return a risk level, a recommended action, and a short explanation based only on the supplied account and policy information. PROMPT; } public function schema ( JsonSchema $schema ): array { return [ 'risk' => $schema -> string () -> required (), 'recommended_action' => $schema -> string () -> required (), 'reason' => $schema -> string () -> required (), ]; } } The response can then be accessed like an array: $response = ( new RefundDecision ) -> prompt ( 'Evaluate refund request RF-1084.' , provider : [ Lab :: OpenAI , Lab :: Anthropic , ], ); $action = $response [ 'recommended_action' ]; This is stronger than “please return JSON” because the output structure becomes part of the agent definition. It still should not be the final validation layer. Convert Model Output Into a Domain Type A string can satisfy the schema and still contain an unsupported business value. The application should reject anything outside its own vocabulary: enum RefundRisk : string { case Low = 'low' ; case Medium = 'medium' ; case High = 'high' ; } enum RefundAction : string { case Approve = 'approve' ; case Review = 'review' ; case Reject = 'reject' ; } final readonly class RefundResult { public function __construct ( public RefundRisk $risk , public RefundAction $action , public string $reason , ) {} public static function fromAiResponse ( $response ): self { return new self ( risk : RefundRisk :: from ( $response [ 'risk' ]), action : RefundAction :: from ( $response [ 'recommended_action' ] ), reason : $response [ 'reason' ], ); } } Now manual_review , approve_now , or an empty value fails before it reaches refund logic. That failure is useful. It protects the business operation from a response that is valid JSON but invalid for the application. Test Every Provider as a Primary Provider A test that always uses the normal provider does not test failover. Run a small contract suite against each configured provider independently: $providers = [ Lab :: OpenAI , Lab :: Anthropic , ]; foreach ( $providers as $provider ) { $response = ( new RefundDecision ) -> prompt ( 'Account is seven days old. Policy requires review.' , provider : $provider , ); $result = RefundResult :: fromAiResponse ( $response ); expect ( $result -> risk ) -> toBeInstanceOf ( RefundRisk :: class ); expect ( $result -> action ) -> toBe ( RefundAction :: Review ); } Keep this separate from fast unit tests because it makes real provider calls. Run it in staging, before changing models, and after upgrading the SDK. Also test what happens when validation fails. The safe behavior might be to retry once, send the request to manual review, or stop the workflow. It should not silently invent a default action. A Backup Provider Is a Different Dependency The important lesson is not that Laravel’s failover failed. It worked exactly where it was supposed to work. The mistake was treating two probabilistic providers as interchangeable implementations of the same deterministic interface. If you are evaluating the best Laravel development company for an AI-enabled application, ask how the team tests structured outputs across every fallback provider. At Spaculus Software, provider availability and business-contract validity are treated as separate production concerns. A 200 OK means the provider answered. It does not mean your application received an answer it can safely use. What contract would break first if your Laravel application switched AI providers today?
